```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", echo = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      warning = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2, out.width = "100%")
library(ggplot2)
ss <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "simstudy.rds", package = "MixSIARPFN"))
sc <- ss$scores
set_lab <- c(geese = "Geese-like", wolves = "Wolves-like,\ndiets from the prior",
             wolves_realistic = "Realistic\nwolves-like")
set_lab1 <- gsub("\n", " ", set_lab)
cols <- c(MixSIAR = "grey35", MixSIARPFN = "#D55E00")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
            theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
                  legend.position = "top"))
pct <- function(x, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%+.", d, "f%%"), 100 * x)

# Compare on the datasets where MixSIAR's long run converged (largest PSRF at most 1.1)
ok <- unique(sc[sc$method == "MixSIAR long" & sc$converged, c("set", "dataset")])
cmp <- merge(sc, ok)
per_ds <- aggregate(cbind(crps, width) ~ set + dataset + method, cmp, mean)
wide <- reshape(per_ds, idvar = c("set", "dataset"), timevar = "method", direction = "wide")

# CRPS of a network version relative to MixSIAR long, with a bootstrap 95% interval
gap <- function(s, v, ref = "MixSIAR long", B = 4000) {
  w <- wide[wide$set == s, ]
  p <- w[[paste0("crps.MixSIARPFN ", v)]]
  m <- w[[paste0("crps.", ref)]]
  keep <- !is.na(p) & !is.na(m)
  p <- p[keep]; m <- m[keep]
  set.seed(1)
  bs <- replicate(B, {i <- sample.int(length(p), replace = TRUE); mean(p[i]) / mean(m[i]) - 1})
  data.frame(set = s, version = v, n = length(p), gap = mean(p) / mean(m) - 1,
             lo = unname(quantile(bs, 0.025)), hi = unname(quantile(bs, 0.975)),
             width = mean(w[[paste0("width.MixSIARPFN ", v)]][keep]) /
               mean(w[[paste0("width.", ref)]][keep]) - 1)
}
gaps <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(set_lab), function(s)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("v1", "v2", "q3", "v3"), function(v) gap(s, v)))))
gr <- gaps[gaps$version == "v3", ]          # the released networks
rownames(gr) <- gr$set
n_all <- sapply(names(set_lab), function(s) length(unique(sc$dataset[sc$set == s])))
g1 <- gaps[gaps$version == "v1", ]
med_min <- with(ss$mixsiar_seconds[ss$mixsiar_seconds$length %in% c("normal", "long"), ],
                range(tapply(seconds, paste(set, length), median)) / 60)
ratio <- wide$`crps.MixSIARPFN v3` / wide$`crps.MixSIAR long`
# Speed: MixSIARPFN fit times (through the package) against MixSIAR's run times
pt <- ss$pfn_seconds
mts <- ss$mixsiar_seconds[ss$mixsiar_seconds$length %in% c("normal", "long"), ]
pfn_med <- tapply(pt$seconds, pt$set, median)
speedup <- outer(names(set_lab), c("normal", "long"), Vectorize(function(s, l)
  median(mts$seconds[mts$set == s & mts$length == l]) / pfn_med[[s]]))
k <- function(x) format(signif(x, 2), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
# How often MixSIARPFN is the more accurate, against converged long runs
n_conv <- sum(!is.na(ratio))
n_better <- sum(ratio < 1, na.rm = TRUE)
n_within10 <- sum(ratio < 1.1, na.rm = TRUE)
# Convergence of MixSIAR's runs, over all datasets
conv_all <- unique(sc[grepl("^MixSIAR (normal|long)$", sc$method),
                      c("set", "dataset", "method", "converged")])
fail_normal <- mean(!conv_all$converged[conv_all$method == "MixSIAR normal"])
fail_long <- mean(!conv_all$converged[conv_all$method == "MixSIAR long"])
cov_rng <- function(m) range(tapply(cmp$covered[cmp$method == m], cmp$set[cmp$method == m], mean))
```

MixSIARPFN replaces MixSIAR's MCMC with a neural network that has learned, from
millions of simulated datasets, what MixSIAR's posterior looks like. This article
explains what that network is and how it was trained, and then puts it to the test:
`r sum(n_all)` simulated datasets with known true diets, each fitted by MixSIARPFN and
by MixSIAR.

**In short:**

- **Thousands of times faster.** A MixSIARPFN fit took a median of
  `r round(min(pfn_med), 1)` to `r round(max(pfn_med), 1)` seconds; MixSIAR's runs on
  the same data took a median of `r round(med_min[1])` to `r round(med_min[2])`
  minutes. That is `r k(min(speedup))` to `r k(max(speedup))` times faster.
- **Nearly the same answers.** Its posterior means are nearly as close to the true
  diets as converged MixSIAR's, and its accuracy (CRPS) is within about
  `r round(100 * max(gr$gap))`% of a fully converged MixSIAR run on average. On
  `r n_better` of the `r n_conv` datasets (`r round(100 * n_better / n_conv)`%) it is
  *more* accurate than converged MixSIAR, and on `r round(100 * n_within10 / n_conv)`%
  it is within 10%.
- **Honest intervals.** Its 95% intervals contained the true diet
  `r round(100 * cov_rng("MixSIARPFN v3")[1])` to
  `r round(100 * cov_rng("MixSIARPFN v3")[2])`% of the time, as they should (MixSIAR:
  `r round(100 * cov_rng("MixSIAR long")[1])` to
  `r round(100 * cov_rng("MixSIAR long")[2])`%). They are a little more cautious than
  MixSIAR's, `r round(100 * min(gr$width))` to `r round(100 * max(gr$width))`% wider.
- **Always an answer.** There is nothing to converge. MixSIAR's standard ("normal")
  run failed its convergence check on `r round(100 * fail_normal)`% of these datasets,
  and even its long run on `r round(100 * fail_long)`%.

## What the network is

### The idea

MixSIAR defines a full Bayesian model: priors on the diet proportions, the
random-effect SDs and the error terms, and a likelihood for the consumers' tracer
values given the sources. Anything we can write down as a prior and a likelihood we
can also *simulate from*: draw parameters from the prior, then draw a dataset from
the likelihood. A **prior-data fitted network** (PFN; Müller et al. 2022) is trained
on millions of such pairs. It is shown the dataset and asked for the parameters that
made it. Trained this way, with a proper scoring rule, its best possible answer is
the Bayesian posterior itself. It learns to do Bayesian inference for MixSIAR's model
in general, rather than fitting one dataset.

At use, the network reads your data once and returns the posterior, with no chains
to run. Two consequences:

- **Marginal posteriors only.** The network answers one question at a time ("what is
  the posterior of Pack 3's proportion of deer?"), so each proportion gets its own
  posterior. There are no joint draws.
- **It is an approximation.** How close it gets to the true posterior depends on how
  well it was trained. That is what the rest of this article measures.

### Its structure

The network is a transformer in the style of TabPFN (Hollmann et al. 2025), with about
17 million parameters. It sees each dataset as a table:

- **Columns** are the tracers (and any continuous covariate).
- **Rows** are of three kinds:
  - **consumers:** one row per consumer, holding its tracer values;
  - **sources:** one row per source (per source-factor level), holding seven numbers
    per tracer: the mean corrected by the discrimination factor, the source SD, the
    standard error, the discrimination SD, the sample size, the concentration and the
    Dirichlet prior α;
  - **queries:** one row per quantity wanted, such as a global proportion, a level's
    proportion, an effect's SD or `resid.prop`. Each carries a tag saying which.
- **Factor levels** get an embedding drawn at random from a pool, so the network
  treats levels as exchangeable, as MixSIAR's model does. At use, the answer is
  averaged over 8 random draws.

The body is 8 identical layers. In each, the tracer cells of every row exchange
information, then consumers and sources exchange information with each other while
queries read from them, then a small feed-forward network updates every cell. Each
cell is 384 numbers wide. Because rows have no positions, the answer does not depend
on the order of consumers or sources.

The output is a **bar distribution** for each query: a histogram over 1,000 bars
spanning [0, 1] for proportions (finer near 0 and 1), and over [0, 20] for SDs and
`resid.prop`. It can take any shape, including the skewed and bimodal posteriors
mixing models often give.

### Training

There are three networks, one for each error structure (Residual * Process, Residual
only, Process only). Each was trained for 450,000 steps on two NVIDIA L40S GPUs (about
two days), with a fresh batch of simulated datasets at every step, so it never sees
the same dataset twice. The simulations cover everything MixSIARPFN supports:

- 2 to 8 sources and 1 to 4 tracers;
- up to two categorical effects (fixed or random, crossed or nested) and one
  continuous effect;
- sources given by a factor, and concentration dependence;
- 1 to 1,000 consumers.

In version 3, the Residual * Process network was trained for a further 150,000 steps
on a second task as well: predicting a diet one source at a time, each source's share
of what the earlier sources leave. This teaches the network how sources trade off
against each other (where the data fix the sum of two sources but not how it splits),
and it made the network's ordinary marginal posteriors more accurate too, by 1 to 2%
on the wolves-like data below. The other two networks are version 2's.

Data outside this range are refused with a message. The networks are on Zenodo
([doi:10.5281/zenodo.24002247](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24002247)) and are
downloaded on first use.

## How it was tested

The test uses datasets where the true diet is known:

1. **The datasets.** Each set copies a MixSIAR example's design exactly (its sources,
   discrimination factors, concentrations, groups and consumers per group) and
   simulates new consumers from MixSIAR's model. Of 200,000 simulations, the ones
   whose spread of consumers looks most like the real data are kept. There are three
   sets of `r n_all[1]` datasets each:
   - **geese-like:** a fixed effect of group, concentration dependence, Residual only
     error;
   - **wolves-like, diets from the prior:** random region and pack effects, pack nested
     in region, sources by region, Residual * Process error. MixSIAR's prior on the
     random-effect SDs (uniform on 0 to 20) makes many packs' diets almost entirely
     one source;
   - **realistic wolves-like:** the same design with SDs between 0.2 and 2, so diets
     vary between packs as they do in real data.
2. **The fits.** MixSIAR fitted every dataset at its "normal" and "long" run lengths,
   three chains each. A run counts as converged when its largest Gelman–Rubin
   diagnostic is at most 1.1. MixSIARPFN fitted the same files.
3. **The comparison.** On the datasets where MixSIAR's long run converged, every diet
   proportion (global and per group) is scored against its true value:
   - **CRPS** (continuous ranked probability score): the main measure. It rewards a
     posterior that is both centred on the truth and tight around it. Lower is
     better, and it is in the units of the proportion;
   - **95% coverage:** how often the 95% interval contains the truth;
   - **width** of the 95% interval;
   - **RMSE** of the posterior mean.

A converged MixSIAR run is, up to Monte Carlo error, the exact posterior. So it is the
best any method can do with these data, and the gap to it is the network's
approximation error.

## Results

### Speed

```{r speed, fig.height = 3}
sp_t <- rbind(data.frame(set = pt$set, method = "MixSIARPFN", seconds = pt$seconds),
              data.frame(set = mts$set, method = paste("MixSIAR", mts$length), seconds = mts$seconds))
sp_t$method <- factor(sp_t$method, c("MixSIARPFN", "MixSIAR normal", "MixSIAR long"))
sp_t$set <- factor(set_lab1[sp_t$set], rev(set_lab1))
ggplot(sp_t, aes(seconds, set, colour = method)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.height = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.7, seed = 1),
             alpha = 0.35, size = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(MixSIARPFN = "#D55E00", `MixSIAR normal` = "grey60",
                                 `MixSIAR long` = "grey25"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 1, 10, 60, 600, 3600, 4 * 3600),
                labels = c("0.1 s", "1 s", "10 s", "1 min", "10 min", "1 h", "4 h")) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 2))) +
  labs(x = "Time to fit one dataset (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

Each point is one fit. MixSIARPFN's times are for the whole fit through the package
(loading the data, the network and summarising the posterior), with the network
already loaded; MixSIAR's are for `run_model()` with three chains. MixSIARPFN is
`r k(min(speedup[, 1]))` to `r k(max(speedup[, 1]))` times faster than MixSIAR's
normal run and `r k(min(speedup[, 2]))` to `r k(max(speedup[, 2]))` times faster than
its long run. The first fit in an R session takes a few seconds more, to start Python
and load the network.

That speed changes what is practical. Fitting all of MixSIAR's alternative models for
a dataset, every dataset in a large study, or a simulation study like this one takes
seconds to minutes instead of days.

### Accuracy against MixSIAR

```{r gap-plot, fig.height = 3.4}
gp <- gaps
gp$version <- factor(gp$version, c("v1", "q3", "v2", "v3"),
                     c("v1 (first release)", "q3 (trained further on common designs)",
                       "v2", "v3 (released)"))
gp$set <- factor(set_lab1[gp$set], rev(set_lab1))
ggplot(gp, aes(100 * gap, set, colour = version)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = 5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey95") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = 100 * lo, xmax = 100 * hi),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), size = 0.4, linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey80", "grey60", "grey35", "#D55E00"), name = NULL) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2, reverse = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = "CRPS relative to converged MixSIAR (%)", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

Each point is MixSIARPFN's mean CRPS relative to MixSIAR's on the same datasets, with
a bootstrap 95% interval over datasets. 0 means as accurate as MixSIAR; the shaded
band is within 5%. The released networks (v3) are within `r pct(min(gr$gap))` to
`r pct(max(gr$gap))` of fully converged MixSIAR, all within or at the 5% band. The first release (v1) was
`r pct(min(g1$gap), 0)` to `r pct(max(g1$gap), 0)` behind. Training further on
the most common designs (q3) did not help. v3 differs from v2 only in the
Residual * Process network (see Training), so for the geese-like data, which use
Residual only error, v2 and v3 are the same.

```{r summary-table}
summ <- function(s, method) {
  d <- cmp[cmp$set == s & cmp$method == method, ]
  data.frame(coverage = mean(d$covered), width = mean(d$width),
             rmse = sqrt(mean((d$mean - d$truth)^2)), crps = mean(d$crps))
}
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(set_lab), function(s) {
  r <- rbind(cbind(method = "MixSIARPFN", summ(s, "MixSIARPFN v3")),
             cbind(method = "MixSIAR long", summ(s, "MixSIAR long")))
  cbind(set = c(set_lab1[[s]], ""), datasets = c(gr[s, "n"], ""), r)
}))
knitr::kable(tab, digits = c(0, 0, 0, 3, 3, 3, 4), row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Data", "Datasets", "Method", "95% coverage", "Width", "RMSE", "CRPS"),
             caption = "Over every diet proportion, on the datasets where MixSIAR's long run converged.")
```

MixSIARPFN's intervals contain the truth at least as often as they should, and on
geese-like data more reliably than MixSIAR's. Its posterior means are nearly as close
to the truth as MixSIAR's (RMSE). Most of the small CRPS difference comes from its
slightly more cautious intervals.

### Dataset by dataset

```{r scatter, fig.height = 3.3}
sp <- wide[!is.na(wide$`crps.MixSIAR long`), ]
sp$set <- factor(set_lab[sp$set], set_lab)
better <- tapply(sp$`crps.MixSIARPFN v3` < sp$`crps.MixSIAR long`, sp$set, mean)
ggplot(sp, aes(`crps.MixSIAR long`, `crps.MixSIARPFN v3`)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(colour = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.6, size = 1.6) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~ set) + coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "MixSIAR long: mean CRPS", y = "MixSIARPFN: mean CRPS")
```

Each point is one dataset (its mean CRPS over all proportions). Points above the line
are datasets where MixSIAR did better, below it datasets where MixSIARPFN did. The
two track each other closely. MixSIARPFN is the more accurate on `r n_better` of
`r n_conv` datasets (`r round(100 * min(better))` to `r round(100 * max(better))`%
by set), within 10% of MixSIAR on `r n_within10`, and on half of them within
`r round(100 * (median(ratio, na.rm = TRUE) - 1))`%. Its largest shortfalls are where
MixSIAR's posterior is very tight (the lower left of the geese-like panel): there
MixSIARPFN stays more cautious, and on `r sum(ratio > 1.75, na.rm = TRUE)` datasets
its CRPS is close to twice MixSIAR's.

### Posterior means against the truth

```{r truth, fig.height = 5}
tp <- cmp[cmp$method %in% c("MixSIARPFN v3", "MixSIAR long"), ]
tp$method <- factor(sub(" v3| long", "", tp$method), c("MixSIAR", "MixSIARPFN"))
tp$set <- factor(set_lab[tp$set], set_lab)
ggplot(tp, aes(truth, mean, colour = method)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols, guide = "none") +
  facet_grid(method ~ set) + coord_equal() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = "True proportion", y = "Posterior mean")
```

Every diet proportion in every dataset. The two panels are hard to tell apart: the two
methods make the same estimates and the same kind of errors, pulling proportions the
data cannot pin down towards the middle, as the prior says they should.

### Interval widths

```{r widths, fig.height = 3.3}
ggplot(sp, aes(`width.MixSIAR long`, `width.MixSIARPFN v3`)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(colour = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.6, size = 1.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ set) + coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "MixSIAR long: mean 95% interval width",
       y = "MixSIARPFN: mean 95% interval width")
```

The points sit close to the line, a little above it: MixSIARPFN's intervals are
typically `r round(100 * min(gr$width))`–`r round(100 * max(gr$width))`% wider. The
network allows for its own approximation error, which keeps its intervals honest.

### Accuracy by true diet proportion

```{r by-truth, fig.height = 3.6}
bp <- cmp[cmp$method %in% c("MixSIARPFN v3", "MixSIAR long"), ]
bp$band <- cut(bp$truth, c(-0.01, 0.02, 0.1, 0.9, 1.01),
               c("below 0.02", "0.02 to 0.1", "0.1 to 0.9", "above 0.9"))
bt <- aggregate(crps ~ set + band + method, bp, mean)
bt$method <- factor(sub(" v3| long", "", bt$method), c("MixSIAR", "MixSIARPFN"))
bt$set <- factor(set_lab[bt$set], set_lab)
ggplot(bt, aes(band, crps, fill = method)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge2(padding = 0.15), width = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols, name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ set) +
  labs(x = "True proportion", y = "Mean CRPS") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

The two are close across the whole range of true proportions. The one pattern to know
about is near 0: where the data cannot rule a source out, MixSIARPFN tends to put a
little more probability close to 0 than MixSIAR does (see the geese example).

### MixSIAR's own convergence and run time

```{r mixsiar-table}
conv <- unique(sc[grepl("^MixSIAR (normal|long)$", sc$method), c("set", "dataset", "method", "converged")])
mt <- ss$mixsiar_seconds
mt <- mt[mt$length %in% c("normal", "long"), ]
ct <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(set_lab), function(s) data.frame(
  set = set_lab1[[s]],
  conv_normal = mean(conv$converged[conv$set == s & conv$method == "MixSIAR normal"]),
  conv_long = mean(conv$converged[conv$set == s & conv$method == "MixSIAR long"]),
  t_normal = median(mt$seconds[mt$set == s & mt$length == "normal"]) / 60,
  t_long = median(mt$seconds[mt$set == s & mt$length == "long"]) / 60)))
knitr::kable(ct, digits = c(0, 2, 2, 0, 0), row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Data", "Converged, normal", "Converged, long",
                           "Minutes, normal", "Minutes, long"),
             caption = "Share of MixSIAR runs that converged, and median run time (three chains).")
```

The comparisons above use only datasets where MixSIAR's long run converged, which is
the fairest test for MixSIAR. In practice MixSIAR's "normal" run, the length most
analyses use, failed its convergence check on `r round(100 * fail_normal)`% of these
datasets, most often with nested random effects, and would have to be rerun longer.
MixSIARPFN has nothing to converge and gives its answer in under a second.

Against MixSIAR's normal run, on the datasets where it converged:

```{r normal-table}
gn <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(set_lab), function(s) {
  okn <- unique(sc[sc$set == s & sc$method == "MixSIAR normal" & sc$converged, "dataset"])
  w <- wide[wide$set == s & wide$dataset %in% okn, ]
  data.frame(set = set_lab1[[s]], n = nrow(w),
             gap = mean(w$`crps.MixSIARPFN v3`) / mean(w$`crps.MixSIAR normal`) - 1)
}))
gn$gap <- pct(gn$gap)
knitr::kable(gn, row.names = FALSE, col.names = c("Data", "Datasets", "MixSIARPFN CRPS relative to MixSIAR normal"))
```

## What this means for use

- MixSIARPFN gives posteriors that are nearly the same as a fully converged MixSIAR
  run, and more accurate on about a third of datasets, in under a second instead of
  an hour or more. It never needs rerunning for convergence.
- Its intervals are honest: they cover the truth at least as often as they claim.
- The speed makes new things practical: fitting every candidate model, every dataset
  in a large study, or rerunning an analysis whenever the data change.
- It gives marginal posteriors, so it cannot give posteriors of sums or differences
  of proportions, or posterior predictive checks of the model. Where those matter, or
  for a final analysis where small differences in a proportion matter, a MixSIAR run
  is a good complement.

## References

- Hollmann, N., Müller, S., Purucker, L., et al. (2025). Accurate predictions on small
  data with a tabular foundation model. *Nature* 637, 319–326.
- Müller, S., Hollmann, N., Pineda Arango, S., Grabocka, J. and Hutter, F. (2022).
  Transformers can do Bayesian inference. *ICLR*.
- Stock, B. C., Jackson, A. L., Ward, E. J., Parnell, A. C., Phillips, D. L. and
  Semmens, B. X. (2018). Analyzing mixing systems using a new generation of Bayesian
  tracer mixing models. *PeerJ* 6:e5096.

The simulation study's results are in `system.file("extdata", "simstudy.rds",
package = "MixSIARPFN")`; `r ss$notes`
